trial_name: CRASH-3 — Tranexamic Acid in Acute Traumatic Brain Injury (2019)
citation: The CRASH-3 trial collaborators. Effects of tranexamic acid on death, disability, vascular occlusive events and other morbidities in patients with acute traumatic brain injury (CRASH-3): a randomised, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet. 2019;394:1713–23.
one_liner: Early tranexamic acid in adult TBI within 3 hours modestly reduces head injury-related death, with clearest benefit in mild-to-moderate injury and reactive pupils, without excess vascular occlusive events.

pico.population: Adults with TBI within 3 hours of injury, GCS ≤12 or any intracranial bleeding on CT, excluding major extracranial bleeding
pico.intervention: Tranexamic acid 1 g IV loading dose over 10 min, followed by 1 g IV infusion over 8 h
pico.comparison: Matching placebo (same loading and infusion regimen)
pico.outcome: Head injury-related death in hospital within 28 days (primary); disability, vascular occlusive events, seizures, other morbidities

background.existing_knowledge: Progressive intracranial haemorrhage after TBI is common and associated with death/disability. TXA reduces surgical bleeding and bleeding deaths in trauma with major extracranial haemorrhage (CRASH-2). Two small TBI trials suggested possible mortality reduction (RR 0.63; 95% CI 0.40–0.99).
background.knowledge_gap: Lack of high-quality evidence on TXA’s effect on TBI-specific death and disability and its safety profile.
background.hypothesis: Early TXA reduces head injury-related death by limiting haemorrhage expansion, with greatest benefit in patients with salvageable injury and within 3 hours.

methods.design: International, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled pragmatic trial
methods.setting: 175 hospitals in 29 countries; predominantly emergency department/acute hospital setting

inclusion: Within 3 hours of injury (after protocol amendment; originally 8 h)
GCS ≤12 or any intracranial bleeding on CT
Clinician substantially uncertain about TXA appropriateness
exclusion: Clinician not substantially uncertain about giving TXA

methods.intervention: Tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 min, then 1 g IV over 8 h
methods.comparison: Matching placebo (1 g‑equivalent volume loading and infusion)
methods.blinding: Patients, clinicians, outcome assessors masked; identical treatment packs; allocation by selecting numbered pack from box
methods.sample_size_power: 10,000 to provide 90% power (two‑sided α=1%) to detect 15% relative reduction in mortality from 20% to 17%; later increased to 13,000 to ensure ~10,000 treated within 3 h
methods.primary_outcome: Head injury‑related death in hospital within 28 days (among those treated within 3 h)
secondary_outcomes: Disability (inability to wash or dress, DRS)

headline_bullets: Primary outcome (head injury‑related death within 3 h) not statistically significant (RR 0.94; 95% CI 0.86–1.02).
Excluding moribund patients (GCS 3, bilateral unreactive pupils) showed borderline benefit (RR 0.89; 0.80–1.00).
Significant benefit in mild‑to‑moderate TBI (GCS 9–15): RR 0.78 (0.64–0.95), and in reactive pupils: RR 0.87 (0.77–0.98).
No excess vascular occlusive events; seizure risk slightly increased but not significant.

outcomes_table.outcome: Primary: head injury‑related death within 28 days (treated within 3 h, ITT)
Sensitivity: head injury‑related death, excluding GCS 3 and bilateral unreactive pupils (within 3 h)
Head injury‑related death within 24 h (treated within 3 h)
outcomes_table.note: Early benefit consistent with bleeding‑related deaths

outcomes_table.outcome: All vascular occlusive events (treated within 3 h)
Disability: unable to wash or dress (within 3 h)
Disability Rating Scale (DRS) among survivors (within 3 h)

subgroup_table.subgroup: Time to treatment ≤1 h (head injury‑related death)
Time to treatment >1–3 h (head injury‑related death)
Time to treatment >3 h (head injury‑related death)

safety: No clear excess vascular occlusive events (RR 1.13, 95% CI 0.80–1.59)
Seizures not significantly increased (RR 1.21, 95% CI 0.94–1.56 within 3 h; all‑patient RR 1.09, 0.90–1.33)

domains.notes: Allocation by selection of identical, numbered pack from box; no foreknowledge; masking applied to all parties.
Unmasking in 13 patients (6 TXA, 7 placebo) unlikely to bias; loading dose given in >98% both arms.
Missing primary outcome data in 37/4613 (0.8%) TXA vs 34/4514 (0.8%) placebo; ITT analysis using available outcomes.
Loading dose given to 98.6% vs 98.7%; maintenance dose to 93.4% vs 92.9%; high adherence.
Well balanced: mean age ~42, ~81% male, GCS categories and pupil reactivity similar.
Clinician‑assigned cause of death, masked, but non‑differential misclassification possible.

internal_validity.verdict: Moderate-to-strong internal validity: robust randomisation, masking, high adherence, minimal missing data, but mid‑trial protocol change and reliance on clinician‑assigned cause of death introduce interpretive complexity.

domains.notes: Adults with suspected TBI across 175 hospitals in 29 countries, wide range of settings, typical trauma demographics (mean age ~42, ~80% male).

Broad severity spectrum; benefit concentrated in mild‑to‑moderate injury and reactive pupils. Excluded major extracranial bleeding, so not generalisable to polytrauma with shock. Intervention simple, time‑dependent, requires IV access. Not studied in children, penetrating TBI, or delayed presentation >3 h.

external_validity.verdict: Good external validity for adult blunt TBI patients who can receive IV TXA within 3 hours and without major extracranial bleeding; limited for paediatric, penetrating, or delayed‑presentation TBI.

strengths: Very large, international, pragmatic, double‑blind RCT
High protocol adherence to the TXA dosing regimen
Prespecified sensitivity analyses to address dilution by moribund patients
limitations: Mid‑trial protocol amendment (time window change and primary endpoint focus) adds interpretive complexity
Primary endpoint reliant on clinician‑assigned cause of death; non‑differential misclassification may attenuate effect
Disability assessed at discharge/28 days, too early for long‑term neurological recovery
Vascular occlusive events captured with high‑specificity criteria, may underestimate total incidence

critical_appraisal.summary: CRASH-3 is a large, well‑conducted trial with moderate internal validity marred by protocol changes and reliance on cause‑specific mortality. The overall signal of benefit is modest and most consistent in less severely injured patients, supporting a time‑sensitive mechanism. The findings are consistent with a small but clinically relevant reduction in head injury‑related death when TXA is given early, without major safety concerns.
weaknesses: Clinician‑assigned cause of death may misclassify

sections.authors_conclusion: TXA should be considered an early intervention for eligible adult TBI patients, with maximal benefit when given as soon as possible and within 3 hours. Benefit concentrated in milder physiological severity (GCS 9–15) and reactive pupils. No clear excess vascular occlusive events; seizure risk compatible with no effect or modest harm.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Early tranexamic acid (1 g bolus + 1 g infusion) within 3 hours of TBI reduces head injury‑related death, especially in patients with GCS 9–15 and reactive pupils, without significant safety concerns. It should be considered in adult TBI patients without major extracranial bleeding.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adults with blunt TBI, GCS ≤12 or intracranial bleed on CT, within 3 hours of injury, no major extracranial haemorrhage
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: TXA does not benefit patients with severe TBI (GCS 3–8) or non‑reactive pupils, and it does not replace standard neurosurgical care.
implementation_caveats: Time‑critical: best within 3 hours, ideally ≤1 hour
Not studied in paediatric or penetrating TBI
Monitor for seizures, though risk not significantly increased
Exclude patients with major extracranial bleeding (use CRASH‑2 evidence for polytrauma)

controversies.notes: Lancet Comment argued that 28‑day head injury‑related mortality may bias towards null, advocate for early bleeding‑related endpoints.
Risk of over‑interpreting mild‑to‑moderate subgroup without stringent interaction thresholds; heterogeneity within ‘severe’ TBI complicates interpretation.
Patients treated earlier may be more severely injured, obscuring an ‘earlier‑is‑better’ effect; adjusted models preferred.
Potential misclassification and interpretive bias; trialists argued blind misclassification biases towards null.
Misclassification of cause of death would bias towards null, not create spurious benefit; defended analytic choices.

context_related_trials.relation: Demonstrated TXA reduces bleeding deaths in trauma with major extracranial haemorrhage, providing the rationale for CRASH‑3 in isolated TBI.

unresolved_questions: Optimal dosing and regimen (e.g., single bolus, different infusion durations)
Benefit in very severe TBI (GCS 3–8, non‑reactive pupils)
Effect of prehospital administration (e.g., by paramedics)

numbers_to_remember: Primary: head injury‑related death 18.5% vs 19.8% (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.86–1.02)
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: For adults with TBI within 3 hours, give TXA 1 g bolus + 1 g infusion; it probably reduces head injury‑related death, especially in less severe injury and reactive pupils, without significant harm.
